11140:
Negligence is the failure to take the care that a sensible, responsible person would reasonably take in a given situation — when that failure causes harm, or creates a serious risk of harm, to someone.

The single most important thing to understand about negligence is this: it is not about doing something bad on purpose. It is about not doing enough — or doing something carelessly — when you had a responsibility to be careful.

Think of it this way: when you act negligently, you didn't wish for anything bad to happen. You simply didn't bother to think carefully, or you knew you should have been more careful but weren't. The harm was the result of your inattention, indifference, or lack of effort, not your intention.
Breaking It Down: The Three Building Blocks

Whenever negligence exists, three things are almost always present:

1. A duty to be careful
The person had a responsibility — sometimes because of their job, their role, or simply because they were in a situation where carelessness could hurt others. A driver has a duty to drive carefully. A doctor has a duty to treat patients with proper medical skill. A shop owner has a duty to keep the floor safe for customers.

2. A failure to meet that duty
The person did not live up to that standard of care. They fell below what a reasonable, ordinary person would have done. Maybe they acted too hastily. Maybe they ignored warning signs. Maybe they simply didn't bother to check.

3. Harm as a result
Because of that failure, someone or something was harmed. The harm was not random or unconnected — it flowed from the carelessness.
The "Reasonable Person" Standard

A critical concept tied to negligence is the idea of the reasonable person. To judge whether someone was negligent, you ask: What would a sensible, careful, ordinary person have done in that same situation?

This is not an impossibly high bar. It doesn't ask whether you are a superhero or an expert. It just asks whether you behaved the way a thoughtful, average person would. If you fell short of that, you may have been negligent.

For example: a reasonable person driving in heavy rain would slow down. Someone who keeps driving at high speed and causes an accident has likely been negligent — not because they wanted to crash, but because they didn't exercise the care that any sensible driver would have.
Everyday Examples

• A construction worker leaves a sharp tool on the floor of a shared hallway. A colleague trips and gets injured. The worker's failure to secure equipment is negligence.
  • A parent leaves a young child unattended near a swimming pool, and the child nearly drowns. Failing to supervise a child in a dangerous environment is negligence.
  • A restaurant employee doesn't clean up a spill, puts up no warning sign, and a customer slips and breaks their wrist. The employee's (or the restaurant's) inaction is negligence.
  • A pharmacist gives a customer the wrong medication because they didn't check the prescription carefully. That careless error is negligence.

In all of these cases, no one meant to cause harm. But harm happened — or could have happened — because someone simply didn't take enough care when they should have.
Negligence in Everyday Speech vs. Legal Contexts

The word is used in two main ways:

In everyday conversation, it simply means carelessness, a lack of proper attention, or irresponsibility. If someone says, "The whole accident happened because of your negligence," they mean: you weren't careful enough, and something went wrong because of it.

In law, negligence is a formal concept and one of the most common grounds for civil lawsuits. If someone's negligence causes you loss or injury, you may have the legal right to claim compensation. Legal negligence requires all three elements (duty, breach, harm) to be proven. Courts use it extensively in cases involving accidents, medical errors, faulty products, and professional failures.
Degrees of Negligence

Not all negligence is equal. Depending on how serious the carelessness is, it can be described at different levels:

Ordinary negligence is the basic form — simply failing to be as careful as a reasonable person would be. A distracted driver who runs a red light and dents your car has been ordinarily negligent.

Gross negligence is a far more serious level — extreme, shocking carelessness that shows a complete disregard for the safety of others. It is not just "I forgot to be careful"; it is "I was so reckless that it was almost as if I didn't care at all whether someone got hurt." A surgeon who operates while heavily intoxicated is a classic example.

Criminal negligence goes one step further. Here, the carelessness is so severe, and the person so obviously indifferent to the danger they were creating, that the law treats it as a criminal act, not just a civil wrong. This can result in imprisonment, not just compensation. A driver who leaves a child locked in a hot car on a summer day and the child dies may face criminal negligence charges.
Types of Negligence (by Context)

Medical negligence (also called clinical negligence or medical malpractice): When a healthcare professional — a doctor, nurse, surgeon, or dentist — fails to provide the standard of care expected in their field, and a patient is harmed as a result. A doctor who misses an obvious diagnosis, a surgeon who operates on the wrong limb, or a pharmacist who dispenses the wrong dose are examples.

Professional negligence: When any trained professional — a lawyer, architect, accountant, engineer — fails to apply the skill and care expected in their profession. A lawyer who misses a critical filing deadline, causing their client to lose a case, has been professionally negligent.

Contributory negligence: A concept where the victim themselves was also partly careless and contributed to their own harm. For example, if you sue a shop for a wet floor injury but you were also running and ignoring warning signs, a court might reduce your compensation because you also bore some of the responsibility.

Comparative negligence: Similar to contributory, this is a legal principle where the total fault is divided between the parties. Perhaps the shop is 70% responsible and you are 30% responsible for your injury, and your compensation is adjusted accordingly.
What Negligence Is NOT — Crucial Distinctions

Understanding what negligence isn't is just as important as knowing what it is.

Negligence ≠ Accident
A pure accident is something that no amount of reasonable care could have prevented. If a freak gust of wind blows a tree onto a car, that's an accident — nobody was negligent. But if the same tree had been visibly rotting for months and the property owner never removed it, its fall is not an accident — that's negligence.

Negligence ≠ Intentional wrongdoing
If someone deliberately pushes you down the stairs, that is intentional harm — a different and far more serious category of wrongdoing. Negligence, by definition, does not involve the desire to harm. The negligent person did not want anything bad to happen; they just didn't take care to prevent it.

Negligence ≠ Recklessness
Recklessness sits between negligence and intentional harm. A reckless person knows about a serious risk and consciously decides to ignore it anyway. A negligent person, by contrast, may not have even fully registered the risk — they simply failed to be careful enough. Recklessness is generally considered morally worse because it involves awareness of danger being deliberately brushed aside.

Negligence ≠ Mere mistake
Everyone makes mistakes, and not every mistake is negligence. Negligence requires a failure of care — doing something below the standard of a reasonable person. A brilliant surgeon who makes an error despite following every proper procedure may have made a mistake, but if they did everything a careful surgeon should do, it is not negligence. On the other hand, if they skipped standard safety checks and then made an error, that failure of care makes it negligence.
Words and Phrases That Commonly Go with "Negligence"

These are the collocations — the natural pairings — that will help you use and recognise the word fluently:

  • Gross negligence — extreme, shocking carelessness
  • Criminal negligence — carelessness serious enough to be a crime
  • Medical negligence / Professional negligence — negligence in a specific field
  • Contributory negligence — the victim also played a role
  • Act of negligence — a specific careless action
  • Prove negligence — establish in court that someone was negligent
  • A claim of negligence — a legal complaint based on negligence
  • Found guilty of negligence — a legal verdict
  • Due to negligence — as a result of carelessness
  • Negligence on the part of — the negligence belonging to a specific person
The Feeling Behind the Word

If you want to grasp the emotional register of "negligence" — how it feels when used — it carries a tone of blame, but a specific kind. It doesn't say "you are evil." It says "you were irresponsible. You should have known better. You had a duty to take care, and you didn't, and someone suffered for it."

It is a word often used in serious situations — medical failures, accidents, professional misconduct, legal disputes. It implies that the harm that occurred was preventable, which is what makes it feel accusatory. The underlying message is: this didn't have to happen.
Summary in One Paragraph

Negligence is the failure to exercise the care, attention, and caution that a reasonable person would have exercised in the same circumstances, where that failure leads to harm or the risk of harm. It is not intentional wrongdoing, and it is not a pure unavoidable accident — it sits in between. It implies responsibility, a falling short of expected standards, and a connection between that carelessness and the harm that followed. The greater the carelessness, the more serious the negligence — from ordinary to gross to criminal. In law, negligence is one of the primary foundations for seeking compensation when someone else's carelessness hurts you. In everyday language, it is simply a serious word for inexcusable carelessness.
11141:
Negligent describes a person (or their behavior) that fails to take the reasonable care that the situation requires — and because of that failure, harm, damage, or risk results (or could result).

In simple words: a negligent person didn't do what a responsible, careful person would have done — and that carelessness caused (or could cause) a problem.
The Big Idea Hidden Inside the Word

The most important thing to understand about "negligent" is that it is not about bad intentions. A negligent person didn't necessarily want anything bad to happen. They simply didn't pay enough attention, didn't try hard enough, or didn't care enough to prevent it.

This is what makes negligent different from words like deliberate or intentional. A deliberate wrongdoer plans to cause harm. A negligent person causes harm through carelessness, inattention, or irresponsibility — they just didn't bother to be careful enough when they should have been.

The word negligent always involves an invisible measuring stick: what would a reasonable, responsible person have done in the same situation?

If someone falls far below that standard — they ignored obvious risks, skipped important duties, or simply didn't try — they are negligent.

This is not a test of perfection. Nobody is expected to be flawless. It's a test of ordinary, sensible carefulness. When someone can't even meet that basic bar, the word negligent applies.

• A babysitter who leaves a toddler alone near a swimming pool and goes inside to watch TV is being negligent. She had a duty to keep the child safe, and she ignored it.
  • A chef who doesn't wash his hands after handling raw meat and then prepares food for customers is being negligent. Basic hygiene is a clear responsibility, and he ignored it.
  • A driver who sends text messages while driving is negligent. Every driver has a duty to pay attention to the road. Texting removes that attention entirely.
  • A pharmacist who gives a patient the wrong medication because she was distracted and didn't double-check the prescription is negligent. Her job required careful checking, and she failed to do it.

Notice that in none of these cases did the person want to cause harm. But they were all dangerously careless in situations where carefulness was absolutely required of them.
Negligent in Formal and Legal Contexts

The word "negligent" is extremely common in legal, medical, and professional settings, because these are fields where people have formal, serious duties of care toward others.

  • A doctor who misses an obvious diagnosis because they didn't bother to run standard tests may be called negligent.
  • A construction company that doesn't follow safety codes, leading to a worker's injury, is negligent.
  • A lawyer who misses a critical deadline for their client because they forgot to check their calendar is negligent.

In law, negligent behavior is one of the most common reasons people are sued. If someone's negligence causes you financial loss, physical injury, or other real harm, the law may hold them responsible — even though they never meant to hurt you.

Not all negligence is equal. There are different intensities:

Slightly negligent — A small lapse in care that a reasonable person might occasionally make, with minor consequences. Example: a waiter who forgets to warn a customer about a slightly slippery floor.

Negligent (standard) — A clear failure to take care that a responsible person would have taken, causing real harm. Most everyday and legal uses fall here.

Grossly negligent — An extreme, shocking level of carelessness, almost approaching recklessness. This is when someone ignores an obvious and serious danger in a way that shows almost total disregard for others' safety. Example: a truck driver who operates a vehicle without functioning brakes because fixing them "costs too much."

The adjective gross is often placed before negligent to signal this highest level of severity.
What Negligent Is NOT — Important Distinctions

Negligent ≠ Accidental
A pure accident can happen even when someone is being fully careful and responsible. Negligence implies that better care could have prevented the outcome.

Negligent ≠ Intentional/Deliberate
If you deliberately hurt someone, you are malicious or reckless — not just negligent. Negligent behavior is careless, not calculated.

Negligent ≠ Merely Imperfect
Making an honest mistake after genuinely trying your best is not negligence. Negligence is about falling below a basic, reasonable standard — not about failing to be perfect.
How the Word Is Used in a Sentence

"Negligent" typically appears right before a noun, or after a linking verb like "was" or "were":

  • "The negligent contractor left the job site without securing the scaffolding."
  • "The court found the hospital to be negligent in its care of the patient."
  • "Her negligent attitude toward the safety checklist put everyone at risk."

You will also often see it in the phrase "negligent in (doing something)":

  • "He was negligent in monitoring the experiment."
  • "She was negligent in her duties as a supervisor."

Since you'll encounter the whole word family in real life:

  • Negligence (noun) — the actual behavior or quality of being negligent. "The accident was caused by negligence."
  • Negligently (adverb) — in a negligent manner. "The nurse negligently administered the wrong dosage."
  • Non-negligent — not negligent; used mainly in formal/legal writing to clear someone of careless blame.

If you ever need to recall the word fast:

Negligent means carelessly failing to do what a responsible person should do, in a situation where that failure causes or risks causing harm to others.

That single idea — carelessness in the face of a clear duty, leading to harm — is the entire heart of the word.
11142:
Something is negligible when it is so small, so minor, or so unimportant that it can be safely ignored without making any real difference.

The key idea hiding inside this word is a threshold. Imagine you have a scale that measures how much something matters. Negligible lives at the very bottom of that scale — so close to zero that, for all practical purposes, you can treat it as zero. The thing still technically exists, but it is too tiny or too weak to deserve serious attention.

A simple everyday example: Imagine you are baking a cake, and a single grain of sugar falls on the floor. Does losing that one grain ruin your cake? Of course not. Its effect on the final product is negligible — it exists, yes, but it changes absolutely nothing. Now contrast this with dropping the entire cup of sugar. That is not negligible; that changes everything.

The critical nuance — negligible is always relative: This is the most important thing to understand about this word. Something is not negligible on its own in absolute terms. It is negligible in comparison to something else, or in the context of a specific situation.

A single drop of water is negligible in the ocean, but it is not negligible in a test tube where scientists are measuring a precise experiment. A five-dollar difference in price is negligible when buying a house worth $500,000, but it is not negligible when a child has only six dollars in their pocket. The word only makes sense when you understand the scale of the situation around it.

How it behaves in sentences: The word almost always appears before a noun or after a linking verb like is, was, seems, or remains.

Before a noun: "The drug had negligible side effects." / "There was a negligible difference between the two results."

After a verb: "The damage was negligible." / "The risk remains negligible."

Common real-world uses: You will encounter this word most often in scientific writing, medicine, finance, engineering, and formal analysis — anywhere people need to be precise about whether something is worth worrying about. A doctor might say the chance of a reaction to a vaccine is negligible. A financial analyst might say the impact of a minor fee on a large investment is negligible. A physicist might say that air resistance, for a slow-moving heavy object, is negligible in their calculation.

Negligible vs. zero: Negligible does not mean the thing is absent or nonexistent. It means the thing is present but too small to matter. This is an important distinction, especially in science. A scientist saying "the error is negligible" is not saying there is no error — they are saying the error is small enough to not affect the conclusion.

Negligible vs. minor: Something minor can still deserve some attention — a minor injury still needs a bandage. Something negligible has crossed the threshold where it needs essentially no attention at all.

Negligible vs. insignificant: These are very close in meaning and are often used interchangeably. However, "insignificant" tends to be a broader, more everyday word that can describe anything unimportant. "Negligible" carries a stronger, more precise flavor — it almost always implies a quantitative or measurable smallness (size, amount, risk, difference, effect), and it suggests that careful people have consciously decided the thing can be left out of their calculations. "Negligible" is the more technical, sharper of the two words.

Synonyms (words with very similar meaning): Trivial, trifling, marginal, minimal, imperceptible, insignificant. Among these, negligible is the one most often used when someone wants to sound precise and measured — it implies a judgment has been made, not just a feeling.

Antonyms (words that mean the opposite): Significant, considerable, substantial, notable, meaningful, appreciable. If something is appreciable, it is large enough to be clearly noticed and worth accounting for — the direct opposite of negligible.
The simplest one-sentence summary you can always return to:
Something is negligible if it is so small or unimportant — relative to the situation — that ignoring it completely would not change anything that matters.
11143:
Think of "negotiable" as a label that tells you: this is not final — it can be discussed and changed.

When something is negotiable, it means two or more people are allowed to talk about it, push back on it, and arrive at a version that works better for everyone. Nothing is locked in stone yet.

When something is non-negotiable, the opposite is true — it is fixed, final, and no amount of discussion will change it.

"Negotiable" has three distinct uses as an adjective. All three share the same spirit — something that isn't stuck in place — but in different situations.

1. Open to Discussion or Change (the most common use)

This is the everyday meaning. When terms, prices, rules, conditions, or decisions are described as negotiable, it means they are flexible and can be changed through conversation or bargaining.

Examples:

  • "The asking price is negotiable." → The seller is not demanding exactly that amount. You can make a lower offer and discuss it.
  • "The salary is negotiable." → The employer hasn't set a rigid number. You can talk about it and ask for more.
  • "The deadline is negotiable." → The due date isn't fixed. You may be able to get more time if you ask.
  • "The rules in this household are not negotiable." → The parents are making clear these rules will not be bent or argued with.

Notice how powerful this word is in both directions. Saying something is negotiable opens a door. Saying it is not negotiable firmly closes it.

Key insight: Something being negotiable doesn't mean it will change — it just means there is room to try. The outcome depends on the conversation.

2. Able to Be Passed Through or Crossed (used for physical obstacles)

Here, "negotiable" describes a path, road, or physical challenge that can actually be traveled through or dealt with — even if it is difficult.

Examples:

  • "The mountain trail is barely negotiable after heavy snow." → The trail is difficult, but it can still be crossed.
  • "The river crossing was negotiable by jeep, but not by a regular car." → A jeep could get through it; a regular car could not.
  • "The gap between the two buildings was negotiable with a running jump." → A person could leap across it.

This use is essentially saying: manageable, passable, possible to get through.

3. Able to Be Legally Transferred (used in finance and law)

This is a technical but important use. In finance and law, a "negotiable instrument" is a written document — like a check, a promissory note, or a bill of exchange — that represents money and can be legally handed over (transferred) from one person to another, giving the new holder the full right to collect that money.

Examples:

  • A check made payable to "cash" (rather than to a specific named person) is negotiable — anyone who holds it can cash it.
  • A promissory note (a written promise to pay someone back) is negotiable if it can be passed on to a third party, who then has the right to collect the debt.

The key idea here is transferability — the value and legal rights attached to the document can move from hand to hand, like physical money can.

A non-negotiable instrument, by contrast, is tied to one specific person. Only that person can use it; it cannot be handed to someone else.

All three uses share a common thread: something negotiable is not locked in place.

  • In everyday life: the terms can move through discussion.
  • On a road or path: you can move through it.
  • In finance: the document can move from one person to another.

The word always carries the idea of movement and flexibility — the opposite of something rigid and fixed.

"Negotiable" implies mutual involvement. Something is rarely negotiable in isolation. It almost always implies that two or more parties are involved — a seller and a buyer, an employer and an employee, a debtor and a creditor. The flexibility exists between people.

Degree matters. Something can be fully negotiable (wide open for discussion), partially negotiable (some things can change but not others), or barely negotiable (technically open to discussion, but not by much). Pay attention to how people modify this word in context.

  • "Everything is negotiable." → Maximum flexibility.
  • "Only the timeline is negotiable — the price is fixed." → Partial flexibility.
  • "That clause is non-negotiable." → Zero flexibility on that point.

"Negotiable" signals intent. When someone calls something negotiable, they are essentially inviting a conversation. It is a social signal, not just a description. In a job ad, "salary is negotiable" is an invitation for you to name your number. In a real estate listing, "price negotiable" is an invitation to make an offer below the asking price.

Context shapes the tone. In business and formal settings, "non-negotiable" sounds firm and professional. In personal relationships, it can sound harsh or inflexible, which is why people in those contexts might soften it by saying something like "this is really important to me and I can't compromise on it" — which means the same thing, but more gently.

SituationWhat "Negotiable" Means
Price, salary, terms, rulesCan be discussed and changed
A road, path, or obstacleCan be traveled through or overcome
A financial documentCan be legally transferred to another person

In short: if something is negotiable, it has room to move. If it is non-negotiable, it does not.
11144:
To negotiate means to have a back-and-forth discussion with one or more people in order to reach an agreement that everyone can accept — especially when those people have different or conflicting interests.

Think of it this way: you want one thing, the other person wants something else, and neither of you can simply force the other to give in. So instead of fighting or walking away, you talk it through, offer things, ask for things, and eventually land on a middle ground that works for both of you. That whole process is negotiating.
What Makes It "Negotiating" — and Not Just Talking?

Not every conversation is a negotiation. Three things define it:

1. There are competing interests. Both sides want something, and those wants don't perfectly match. A buyer wants to pay less; a seller wants to earn more. An employee wants a higher salary; a company wants to keep costs low.

2. Both sides have some power. Neither side can simply dictate to the other. If one side can just force the other, there's nothing to negotiate — it's a command. True negotiation only happens when both sides have something the other needs.

3. The goal is a mutual agreement. You're not just arguing. You're working toward a deal. Each side gives something up and gains something in return. This is called a compromise, and it's the usual result of successful negotiation.

"Negotiate" appears in many different areas of life:

In business: Companies negotiate contracts, prices, and deals. "The two companies negotiated a partnership agreement."

In the workplace: Employees negotiate salaries and benefits with employers. "She negotiated a 15% pay raise before accepting the job offer."

In international affairs: Countries negotiate peace treaties, trade agreements, and diplomatic deals. "The two nations negotiated a ceasefire after months of conflict."

In everyday life: Even informal situations count. "The children negotiated over who would get the last slice of pizza." Or: "He negotiated with his landlord to lower the rent."

In legal settings: Lawyers negotiate settlements — agreements reached before a case goes to trial. "The two parties negotiated a settlement out of court."

"Negotiate" also has a second sense that is completely different from agreements and deals. It means to successfully navigate or get through a physical obstacle or difficult situation — usually by handling it with skill and care.

Examples:

  • "The driver carefully negotiated the narrow mountain road." (= steered through it skillfully)
  • "She negotiated the crowded market without bumping into anyone." (= moved through it successfully)
  • "The pilot negotiated the severe storm and landed safely." (= managed through a difficult situation)

In this sense, the "obstacle" takes the place of the "other party," and successfully getting past it takes the place of "reaching a deal." The common thread is: something difficult stood in the way, and you handled it skillfully.

Understanding what negotiation is not makes the meaning much sharper:

  • It is not demanding. Demanding means you simply state what you want and expect the other person to comply. Negotiating means you're open to discussion and compromise.
  • It is not begging. Begging means asking from a position of no power. Negotiating means you have something to offer in return.
  • It is not forcing. If you force someone, there's no discussion. Negotiating requires willingness from both sides.
  • It is not a one-sided conversation. It always involves at least two parties exchanging offers, ideas, or positions.

What truly defines "negotiate" is the spirit of finding middle ground. Both parties come with their own needs, but they respect that the other side has needs too. They talk, they listen, they make offers, they adjust, and they move toward each other — not away. The goal is always an agreement that both sides can live with, even if it's not the perfect outcome for either.

Since you want full mastery of this word, here are its closest relatives:

  • Negotiation (noun) — the process or act of negotiating. "The negotiation lasted three days."
  • Negotiator (noun) — a person who negotiates, especially professionally. "She is a skilled negotiator."
  • Negotiable (adjective) — able to be changed through negotiation; open to discussion. "The price is negotiable." (Its opposite is non-negotiable — meaning it cannot be changed or debated.)
  • Negotiated (past tense / adjective) — "They reached a negotiated settlement."
Common Phrases You'll Hear With This Word

• Negotiate a deal — to work out and agree on a deal
  • Negotiate a contract — to discuss and agree on the terms of a contract
  • Negotiate terms — to discuss the specific conditions of an agreement
  • Negotiate in good faith — to negotiate honestly, with a genuine intention to reach an agreement (not to deceive)
  • Negotiate a raise — to discuss and persuade an employer to increase your salary
  • Hard to negotiate with — describing someone who is stubborn or inflexible in discussions

To negotiate means: to engage in a deliberate, mutual discussion with someone who has different interests, with the aim of reaching an agreement both parties can accept — and less commonly, to skillfully handle or move through a physical obstacle or challenge.
11145:
Negotiation is a conversation between two or more parties who have different interests or needs, with the goal of reaching an agreement that all of them can accept.

Think of it this way: two people want something, they don't fully agree on how to get it, so they talk, exchange offers, and work toward a middle ground. That process — from the first word to the final handshake — is negotiation.
What Makes Something a Negotiation?

Not every conversation is a negotiation. A negotiation has three essential ingredients:

  1. Two or more parties — There must be people (or groups, companies, or countries) on different sides.
  2. A conflict of interest or different positions — Each side wants something the other doesn't immediately agree to give.
  3. A desire to reach an agreement — Both sides must actually want to resolve the difference. If one side refuses to engage at all, there is no negotiation.
The Heart of Negotiation: Positions vs. Interests

This is one of the most important ideas in understanding negotiation deeply.

  • A position is what someone says they want. ("I want ₹50,000 for this car.")
  • An interest is why they want it — the underlying need or motivation. ("I need money to pay a debt by Friday.")

Skilled negotiation looks past positions and tries to understand interests. When both sides understand what each other truly needs, it becomes much easier to find creative solutions that satisfy everyone.

Example: A landlord says the rent is ₹15,000. A tenant says they can only pay ₹12,000. That's a positional conflict. But if the landlord's real interest is reliable, long-term tenancy, and the tenant's real interest is stability at a lower cost, they might agree to ₹12,500 with a two-year lease. Both interests are satisfied even though neither got exactly what they initially stated.
The Two Broad Types of Negotiation

1. Distributive Negotiation (Win-Lose)

This is like dividing a single pie — whatever one person gets, the other loses. There is a fixed amount to be shared. Haggling over the price of something at a market is a classic example. One side's gain is directly the other's loss.

This type tends to be more competitive, with each side trying to claim as much as possible.

2. Integrative Negotiation (Win-Win)

Here, the goal is to expand the pie before dividing it — to find solutions that make both sides better off. This requires understanding each other's interests, sharing some information, and being creative.

This type is more collaborative. It's used in business partnerships, labor agreements, international diplomacy, and long-term relationships where both parties need to keep working together.

Most real-world negotiations contain elements of both — some things are fixed and must be divided, while others can be expanded or traded.
Key Concepts You Must Know

BATNA — Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement

Your BATNA is what you will do if the negotiation fails — your best option outside the negotiation. It is arguably the most powerful concept in all of negotiation.

  • If your BATNA is strong (you have other good options), you have more power — you don't need this deal.
  • If your BATNA is weak (you have no other options), you are under pressure to accept whatever the other side offers.

Example: If you're negotiating a salary and you already have another job offer for ₹80,000, your BATNA is that other offer. This gives you confidence and leverage. If you have no other offer, your BATNA is weak.

Always know your BATNA before entering any negotiation. And try to improve it beforehand if you can.

Reservation Point (Walk-Away Point)

This is the absolute worst deal you would accept before walking away. It is determined by your BATNA. If an offer is worse than your walk-away point, you should not accept — you'd be better off with your alternative.

ZOPA — Zone of Possible Agreement

This is the range where a deal can happen. It exists when one party's walk-away point overlaps with the other's.

Example: You're willing to sell a bicycle for as low as ₹5,000 (your minimum). A buyer is willing to pay as high as ₹7,000 (their maximum). The ZOPA is ₹5,000–₹7,000. Any deal in that range works for both. If your minimum was ₹8,000, there would be no ZOPA, and no deal would be possible.

Anchoring

The first number or offer made in a negotiation acts as an anchor — it powerfully influences all future discussion. People tend to adjust from the anchor rather than think from scratch. This is why whoever makes the first offer often has an advantage — if their anchor is favorable.

Example: If a seller says "₹1,00,000" first, negotiation tends to happen near that number. If the buyer had spoken first and said "₹60,000," the same car might have sold for much less.

Concessions

A concession is when you give up something — move from your original position toward the other side. Concessions are the currency of negotiation. Making a concession signals flexibility and good faith, but doing it too quickly or too freely signals weakness.

Good negotiators:

  • Make concessions slowly and reluctantly
  • Never give something without getting something in return
  • Make smaller and smaller concessions over time (signaling they are near their limit)
Styles of Negotiation

Competitive (Hard bargaining)

The negotiator treats it as a contest to win. They make extreme opening offers, resist concessions, and apply pressure. This works for one-time transactions but damages long-term relationships.

Collaborative (Principled negotiation)

The negotiator focuses on interests, not positions; invents options for mutual gain; and uses objective criteria (market value, legal standards) rather than pressure. This approach, developed by Harvard researchers, leads to better outcomes for both sides and preserves relationships.

Accommodating

The negotiator gives in easily to keep the peace. This can damage their outcome and actually signals weakness to the other side, encouraging more demands.

Avoiding

Refusing to engage at all. This is sometimes strategic (waiting for a better moment), but usually just means the problem remains unsolved.

Most effective real-world negotiators adapt their style based on the situation.
The Stages of a Negotiation

1. Preparation — Research the other side, know your BATNA, decide your walk-away point, understand your interests and theirs.
  2. Opening — Establish the tone. Both sides state their positions. Anchoring happens here.
  3. Exploration — Ask questions, listen, probe for interests behind positions. This is where real information is exchanged.
  4. Bargaining — Offers, counter-offers, and concessions. The actual back-and-forth.
  5. Closing — Agreement is reached (or not). Terms are confirmed.
  6. Commitment — The deal is recorded, formalized, or acted upon.

Preparation is almost always the most neglected stage — and the most important.
Where Negotiation Happens

Negotiation is everywhere:

  • Business: contracts, salaries, vendor pricing, mergers
  • Law: settlements, plea bargains
  • Politics: treaties, trade agreements, coalition formation
  • Personal life: deciding where to vacation with a partner, splitting household responsibilities, buying a house
  • Parenting: even getting a child to eat vegetables involves a form of negotiation

Any time two people have different wants and need to reach a shared decision, negotiation is present.
Common Misconceptions

"Negotiation means being aggressive or manipulative."
No. The most effective negotiators are often calm, curious, and focused on understanding the other side. Aggression tends to trigger defensiveness and break deals.

"There must always be a winner and a loser."
Not true. In integrative negotiation, both sides can genuinely come out better than if they had not negotiated at all.

"You should never make the first offer."
This is overstated. If you're well-prepared, making the first offer lets you anchor the negotiation in your favor.

"Negotiation is only for big decisions."
The same principles apply whether you're negotiating a ₹500 item or a billion-dollar contract. The scale changes; the logic doesn't.
Why Negotiation Matters

Every resource in life — money, time, opportunity, respect — is in some sense negotiated. People who understand negotiation:

  • Get better salaries and deals
  • Resolve conflicts more peacefully
  • Build stronger relationships (because they find solutions that work for everyone)
  • Make better decisions (because they understand what they truly need vs. what they just think they want)

Negotiation is not just a business skill. It is a fundamental life skill — the ability to get what you need from the world while treating others fairly.
One-Sentence Summary

Negotiation is a deliberate, structured conversation between parties with differing interests, aimed at reaching a mutually acceptable agreement — through the exchange of information, offers, and concessions.
11146:
A neigh is the loud, distinctive vocal sound that a horse makes. It is the sound most people immediately think of when they think of a horse — that high-pitched, drawn-out call that rises in pitch and then falls, almost like a musical note that stretches out before fading. If you have ever heard a horse call out loudly from a stable or a field, what you heard was a neigh.

The word itself is onomatopoeic, which means it is spelled and pronounced in a way that mimics the actual sound. When you say the word "neigh" out loud, you are essentially imitating the sound a horse makes.

A neigh is not a quiet sound. It is loud, resonant, and carries over long distances. It has a kind of musical quality — it starts, grows, and then tapers off. It is produced deep in the horse's throat and can feel powerful and almost commanding when you hear it up close. The sound can last anywhere from a fraction of a second to several seconds depending on the horse and the situation.

Each horse's neigh is slightly different, much like how every human voice is unique. Horses can actually recognize each other — and even their owners — by the sound of a neigh.
Why a Horse Produces a Neigh

A neigh is a form of communication. Horses are social animals, and the neigh is their primary long-distance call. Here are the key reasons a horse might let out a neigh:

  • Calling out to another horse. If a horse is separated from a companion or its herd, it will neigh loudly to locate them, as if calling out "Where are you?"
  • Responding to another neigh. If a horse hears another horse neigh in the distance, it will often reply with its own neigh.
  • Greeting or excitement. A horse may neigh when it sees a familiar person approaching, especially if it associates that person with feeding or care.
  • Alertness or unease. When something unfamiliar or startling happens nearby, a horse may neigh as a signal of alertness — almost like an alarm call to others.
  • Anticipation. Horses often neigh at feeding time or just before something they expect and look forward to.

In short, a neigh is the horse's way of making itself heard — whether to connect, respond, warn, or express emotion.
Using "Neigh" as a Noun in Sentences

• "A loud neigh echoed from the stable."
  • "The child jumped when she heard the sudden neigh of the horse."
  • "We could hear the neigh of horses in the distance."
  • "The mare let out a soft neigh when her foal walked near."

Notice that in all these cases, "neigh" is the thing being referred to — the sound itself — rather than the act of making it. That is what makes it a noun: it names the sound as an object of experience.

Horses make a few different sounds, and it is useful to know how a neigh compares:

  • A whinny is closely related to a neigh and the two words are often used interchangeably in everyday language. If there is a difference, a whinny tends to be slightly softer, shorter, and more intimate — like a quiet, friendly greeting — while a neigh is typically louder and more far-reaching. In practice, many people use both words to mean the same thing.
  • A nicker is a much softer, lower, rumbling sound a horse makes in its throat, usually as a close-up greeting — when a horse sees you and gently vocalizes without opening its mouth wide. It is warmer and quieter than a neigh.
  • A snort is a sharp, forceful expulsion of air through the nostrils. It often signals alertness, suspicion, or playfulness.

Of all of these, the neigh is the loudest and most iconic — the sound that defines a horse in most people's minds.

A neigh (noun) is the loud, high-pitched, resonant call of a horse — its primary way of communicating across distances. It is used to locate companions, respond to other horses, express excitement or unease, and announce presence. It is the defining sound of the horse, instantly recognizable, and the word itself is shaped to sound like what it describes.
11147:
"Neighboring" means "located next to or very close to something else."

When you describe something as neighboring, you are saying it is situated right beside, or immediately near, another place or thing — and the two share some kind of proximity, often a common border or boundary.

Think of it this way: if you and your friend both live on the same street, with your houses right next to each other, your house and your friend's house are neighboring houses. They are neighbors to each other.

"Neighboring" is almost always used to describe places, spaces, or areas — things that have a physical location. The most common uses are:

  • Countries: India and Nepal are neighboring countries. (They share a border.)
  • Towns or cities: The fire spread to neighboring villages.
  • Buildings: She moved to a neighboring apartment.
  • Rooms: The noise came from a neighboring room.
  • Regions or territories: The disease affected neighboring states.
  • Seats or tables: A man at a neighboring table was listening to their conversation.

The word tells you: this thing is right there, beside or very near the thing we're already talking about.

"Neighboring" almost always works relative to something already mentioned or understood. It points to something that is close to a known center or place.

For example:

  • "The fire destroyed the library and neighboring shops."
    — Here, the library is the reference point. The "neighboring shops" are the shops that were right next to the library.
  • "Troops moved into neighboring territory."
    — The neighboring territory is territory adjacent to the one being discussed.

So the word doesn't just say "something is somewhere near." It says "something is near this specific thing we're already focusing on."

This is important. "Neighboring" usually means immediately beside or very nearby — typically sharing a border or wall. It is not just "somewhere in the same general area."

  • A room in the same corridor, right next to yours → neighboring room ✓
  • A room on the other side of the building → not really "neighboring"
  • A country that shares a land or sea border → neighboring country ✓
  • A country that is two countries away → not "neighboring"

The closeness implied by "neighboring" is usually the kind where there is direct contact or a shared boundary — or at the very least, no significant gap between the two things.
Can It Be Used in a Slightly Abstract Way?

Yes, occasionally. Sometimes "neighboring" is used for things that are conceptually close or part of the same domain, not just physically close. But this is less common and usually still carries the idea of being "right next to" something.

For example:

  • "Neighboring disciplines like chemistry and biology often overlap."
    — Here, the two fields of study are said to be "neighboring" because they are closely related and touch each other at their edges, just like neighboring countries.

But this abstract use is the exception. In most everyday writing and speech, "neighboring" is about physical or geographic closeness.
Words Similar to "Neighboring" — and How They Differ

Understanding how "neighboring" compares to similar adjectives will sharpen your understanding of it.

Adjacent
"Adjacent" means directly next to something, with no gap at all — usually sharing a wall, edge, or border. It is more precise and formal than "neighboring."

  • The kitchen is adjacent to the dining room. (They share a wall.)
  • "Adjacent" is more clinical and exact. "Neighboring" is warmer and broader.

Adjoining
"Adjoining" means sharing a wall, door, or common boundary. It is even more specific than "adjacent" — it almost always implies physical connection.

  • We booked adjoining rooms at the hotel. (The rooms share a connecting door or wall.)
  • "Neighboring" does not require a physical connection as strongly as "adjoining" does.

Nearby
"Nearby" simply means "not far away." It is vaguer — something can be "nearby" even if it is a few streets away or even across a field. There is no strong implication of a shared border.

  • There is a pharmacy nearby.
  • "Neighboring" implies greater closeness and more of a border-sharing relationship than "nearby."

Bordering
"Bordering" focuses specifically on sharing a defined border, especially for countries or regions.

  • Pakistan and India are bordering nations.
  • "Bordering" is more technical and formal. "Neighboring" is the more natural, everyday word when talking about places near each other.

Summary of the difference:
If you imagine a scale from vaguely near to physically touching, it roughly goes:
Nearby → Neighboring → Adjacent → Adjoining/Bordering

"Neighboring" sits comfortably in the middle — close enough to imply a real, clear proximity, but not so strict as to require a shared wall or exact boundary.

"Neighboring" is a neutral, everyday word. It is neither too formal nor too casual. You will find it in:

  • Newspaper articles ("neighboring towns were also affected")
  • Academic writing ("neighboring nations share a long history")
  • Casual conversation ("ask the people in the neighboring flat")

It is a very natural and common English adjective, and you can use it comfortably in almost any context without worrying about it sounding out of place.
A Few Final Sentences to Fix the Meaning

Read these slowly and notice how "neighboring" works in each one:

  1. The two neighboring farms shared a fence along the hillside. — Two farms right next to each other.
  2. Firefighters stopped the blaze before it reached neighboring houses. — Houses immediately beside the one on fire.
  3. She could hear music coming from a neighboring room. — The room right next to hers.
  4. Aid was sent to the earthquake-hit region and its neighboring areas. — Areas immediately surrounding the affected region.
  5. The small café was popular with workers from the neighboring office building. — The office building right next to the café.

In every case, the pattern is the same: something is right beside or very close to something else, sharing proximity — and often a border.

That is the full, precise meaning of neighboring.
11148:
When someone says something is "neither here nor there," they mean it is irrelevant — it does not matter, it does not change anything, and it has no real connection to the main point being discussed.

Think of it this way: if "here" and "there" represent two important places, something that is neither here nor there exists somewhere outside of both — it is completely out of the picture. It simply does not belong to the conversation in any meaningful way.

In short: "Stop, that point doesn't matter right now."

Imagine two friends arguing about which restaurant to go to tonight. One friend says:

"But I heard the chef at Mario's used to work in France!"

The other replies:

"That's neither here nor there. The question is whether it's within our budget."

The chef's background might be interesting, but it is totally beside the point. It does not help them decide anything. That is exactly what "neither here nor there" captures — a fact or argument that exists outside the boundary of what actually matters.
Breaking Down the Phrase Word by Word

• Neither... nor... — This is a grammatical structure meaning "not this... and not that either." It rules out two things at once.
  • Here — Think of "here" as the core issue, the main point.
  • There — Think of "there" as the other side of the argument or the outcome.

So "neither here nor there" = not connected to the main point, and not connected to the outcome either. It floats somewhere in the middle, touching nothing important.

This idiom has been in the English language for a very long time. It appears in writing as far back as the 16th century. The earliest known recorded use is from the works of Hugh Latimer, an English bishop, around 1546. Later, Shakespeare also used similar phrasing in his plays, which helped cement the expression in the English-speaking world.

The original sense was spatial — "here" and "there" were literal locations. Over time, the phrase evolved into a purely abstract idea, losing its physical meaning entirely and coming to mean simply: this thing belongs nowhere in this discussion.
How and When to Use It

You use this idiom when:

  1. Someone brings up a point that is off-topic and you want to redirect the conversation.
  2. A fact is true but does not change the conclusion in any way.
  3. You want to dismiss something politely without calling it completely wrong.

It is a gentle, non-aggressive way of saying "that's not the point." It does not say the other person is wrong — it simply says what they said does not apply here.

Example 1 — In a meeting:

"Whether he meant to send that email or not is neither here nor there. The damage to the client relationship has already been done."

(It doesn't matter what his intention was — the result is what counts.)

Example 2 — In everyday life:

"I know you studied really hard for the exam. But honestly, that's neither here nor there — you still need to score above 80% to pass."

(Your effort is acknowledged, but it doesn't change the requirement.)

Example 3 — In a debate:

"The fact that the policy worked in Denmark is neither here nor there. Our country has a completely different economic structure."

(What worked somewhere else is irrelevant to this specific situation.)

This phrase is considered neutral to mildly formal. It is not rude, but it is also not especially warm. It is direct and business-like. You can use it comfortably in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Professional or workplace settings
  • Writing (essays, emails, reports)
  • Debates and discussions

It would sound a little too stiff in very casual, playful conversations between close friends, where you might instead simply say "that's beside the point" or "that doesn't matter."

These phrases carry nearly the same meaning and can often be used interchangeably:

  • "That's beside the point" — Very common, slightly more casual.
  • "That's irrelevant" — More blunt and direct.
  • "That doesn't matter here" — Very plain and simple.
  • "That's off the point" — Less common but used the same way.
  • "That's a moot point" — Slightly different: this means the point used to matter but no longer does, or it is debatable but changes nothing practical.

Among all of these, "neither here nor there" is the most idiomatic and has the most literary flavor.

Because the idiom uses the words "here" and "there," some learners mistakenly think it refers to physical locations or directions. It does not. It is always about relevance, not geography. No matter the context, the meaning is always: this does not apply, this does not affect the outcome, this is not the point.

"Neither here nor there" = This point is irrelevant — it does not belong to this discussion and it does not change anything.

Master that core idea, and you will understand this idiom perfectly every single time you encounter it.
11149:
A nemesis is someone or something that brings about another person's downfall, defeat, or ruin — and crucially, this downfall is usually deserved. Think of it as the universe's way of evening the score.

The word carries a powerful sense of inevitability. A nemesis doesn't just cause harm randomly — it is the specific thing that a person cannot escape, no matter how hard they try.

The word "nemesis" is used in three closely related ways:

1. A Rival or Enemy You Cannot Defeat

This is the most common everyday use. Your nemesis is your arch-rival — someone who always seems to get the better of you, who matches or outclasses you every time, and who you simply cannot overcome.

"The detective finally came face to face with his nemesis — the one criminal who had outsmarted him for years."

This kind of nemesis is personal. There's history between the two parties, a repeated clash, and a sense that this one opponent is the specific person you are pitted against in life.

2. The Agent of Your Downfall (A Person, Force, or Thing)

Here, nemesis means the very thing — a person, a flaw, a habit, a situation — that ultimately destroys or ruins someone.

"His arrogance was his nemesis. It cost him everything he had built."

Notice that in this use, the nemesis doesn't have to be a rival. It can be a weakness inside the person themselves, or a force outside them. What matters is that it is the thing responsible for their collapse.

3. A Deserved or Unavoidable Punishment

This meaning is more formal and philosophical. Nemesis refers to a punishment or consequence that is just — meaning the person had it coming. It's the idea that bad actions eventually catch up with you, and the force that makes that happen is called nemesis.

"After years of deceiving others, nemesis finally caught up with him in the form of a public scandal."

This usage echoes the original idea of cosmic justice — the world correcting an imbalance caused by someone's pride, cruelty, or wrongdoing.

Many words describe enemies or failure, but "nemesis" is unique because it bundles several ideas together at once:

  • Inevitability — A nemesis is not just a threat. It is the inescapable one. You sense that sooner or later, this force will catch you.
  • Deserved consequence — There is almost always a moral dimension. The downfall is not just bad luck; it is something the person brought upon themselves through their own flaws or wrongdoing.
  • A perfect match — A nemesis is specifically calibrated to undo you. It targets your exact weakness. What destroys one person would not necessarily destroy another.
  • Dramatic weight — The word carries gravity. Using "nemesis" signals that this is not a minor setback or a casual enemy. This is the defining opposition in someone's story.

Your nemesis doesn't have to be a person. It can be:

  • A person → "She was his nemesis from the very first competition."
  • A personal flaw → "Perfectionism became her nemesis — she never finished anything."
  • A situation or subject → "Calculus was his nemesis throughout university."
  • An abstract force → "Time itself was the artist's nemesis."

As long as the thing consistently defeats, undermines, or ultimately destroys someone — especially in a way that feels deserved or inescapable — you can call it a nemesis.
How It's Used in a Sentence (Varied Examples)

• "The superhero finally defeated his nemesis after a decade of battles." → arch-rival
  • "Overconfidence proved to be Napoleon's nemesis." → the flaw that caused his downfall
  • "She had escaped trouble many times, but nemesis was waiting." → deserved punishment personified as an approaching force
  • "Public speaking has always been my nemesis." → something I consistently fail at or struggle to overcome
One Key Thing to Remember About Tone

"Nemesis" is a serious, weighty word. It belongs in dramatic, significant, or literary contexts. If you use it casually, it can sound either poetic or slightly humorous (as in jokingly calling a subject your nemesis). But in serious writing or speech, it conveys that the conflict or downfall being described is profound, personal, and deeply meaningful — not trivial.

What it isThe ultimate enemy, rival, or cause of someone's ruin
Key qualityDeserved + inescapable
Can refer toA person, a flaw, a force, or an abstract thing
ToneSerious, dramatic, weighty
Pluralnemeses

One sentence to remember it forever: Your nemesis is the one thing the universe has perfectly designed to undo you — and you probably earned it.
